entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.1-1Sam.17.11">1Sa 17:1-11</reference> <div eID="gen3934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3935" type="x-p"/> Some time after David first came to Saul for the purpose of playing, and when he had gone back to his father to Bethlehem, probably because Saul’s condition had improved, the Philistines made a fresh attempt to subjugate the Israelites. They collected their army together (<hi type="italic">machaneh</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.14.24">Exo 14:24</reference>; Jdg 4:16) to war at <hi type="italic">Shochoh</hi>, the present <hi type="italic">Shuweikeh</hi>, in the Wady <hi type="italic">Sumt</hi>, three hours and a half to the south-west of Jerusalem, in the hilly region between the mountains of Judah and the plain of Philistia (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.15.35">Jos 15:35</reference>), and encamped between <hi type="italic">Shochoh</hi> and <hi type="italic">Azekah</hi>, at <hi type="italic">Ephes-dammim</hi>, which has been preserved in the ruins of <hi type="italic">Damûm</hi>, about an hour and a half east by north of Shuweikeh; so that <hi type="italic">Azekah</hi>, which has not yet been certainly traced, must be sought for to the east or north-east of Damûm (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.10.10">Jos 10:10</reference>).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.12-1Sam.17.15">1Sa 17:12-15</reference> <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.12-1Sam.17.15">1Sa 17:12-15</reference> are closely connected with the preceding words, “<hi type="italic">All Israel was alarmed at the challenge of the Philistine; but David the son of that Ephratite</hi> (Ephratite, as in Rth 1:1-2) <hi type="italic">of Bethlehem in Judah, whose name was Jesse</hi>,” etc. The verb and predicate do not follow till <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.15">1Sa 17:15</reference>; so that the words occur here in the form of an anacolouthon. The traditional introduction of the verb היה between ודוד and בּן־אישׁ (David was the son of that Ephratite) is both erroneous and misleading. If the words were to be understood in this way, היה could no more be omitted here than היתה in <reference osisRef="2Chr.22.3">2Ch 22:3</reference>, 2Ch 22:11. The true explanation is rather, that <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.12-1Sam.17.15">1Sa 17:12-15</reference> form one period expanded by parentheses, and that the historian lost sight of the construction with which he commenced in the intermediate clauses; so that he started afresh with the subject ודוד in <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.15">1Sa 17:15</reference>, and proceeded with what he had to say concerning David, doing this at the same time in such a form that what he writes is attached, so far as the sense if concerned, to the parenthetical remarks concerning Jesse’s eldest sons. To bring out distinctly the remarkable chain of circumstances by which David was led to undertake the conflict with Goliath, he links on to the reference to his father certain further notices respecting David’s family and his position at that time. Jesse had eight sons and was an old man in the time of Saul. באנשׁים בּא, “come among the weak.” אנשׁים generally means, no doubt, people or men. But this meaning does not give any appropriate sense here; and the supposition that the word has crept in through a slip of the pen for בּשּׁנים, is opposed not only by the authority of the early translators, all of whom read אנשׁים, but also by the circumstance that the expression בּשּׁנים בּוא does not occur in the whole of the Old Testament, and that ביּמים בּוא alone is used with this signification.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.16-1Sam.17.17">1Sa 17:16-17</reference> <div eID="gen3946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3947" type="x-p"/> The Philistine drew near (to the Israelitish ranks) morning and evening, and stationed himself for forty days (in front of them). This remark continues the description of Goliath’s appearance, and introduces the account which follows. Whilst the Philistine was coming out every day for forty days long with his challenge to single combat, Jesse sent his son David into the camp. “<hi type="italic">Take now for thy brethren this ephah of parched grains</hi> (see <reference osisRef="Lev.23.13">Lev 23:13</reference>), <hi type="italic">and these ten loaves, and bring them quickly into the camp to thy brethren</hi>.”

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.18">1Sa 17:18</reference> <div eID="gen3947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3948" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And these ten slices of soft cheese</hi> (so the ancient versions render it) <hi type="italic">bring to the chief captain over thousand, and visit thy brethren to inquire after their welfare, and bring with you a pledge from them</hi>” - a pledge that they are alive and well. This seems the simplest explanation of the word ערבּתם, of which very different renderings were given by the early translators.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.23">1Sa 17:23</reference> <div eID="gen3951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3952" type="x-p"/> Whilst he was talking with them, the champion (middle-man) Goliath drew near, and spoke according to those words (the words contained in 1Sa 17:8.), and David heard it. פל ממּערות is probably an error for פל ממּערכות (<hi type="italic">Keri</hi>, lxx, <hi type="italic">Vulg.</hi>; cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.26">1Sa 17:26</reference>). If the <hi type="italic">Chethibh</hi> were the proper reading, it would suggest an Arabic word signifying a crowd of men (Dietrich on <hi type="italic">Ges. Lex.</hi>).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.24-1Sam.17.25">1Sa 17:24-25</reference> <div eID="gen3952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3953" type="x-p"/> All the Israelites fled from Goliath, and were so afraid. They said (ישׂראל אישׁ is a collective noun), “<hi type="italic">Have ye seen this man who is coming?</hi> (הרּאיתם, with <hi type="italic">Dagesh dirim</hi> as in 1Sa 10:24. <hi type="italic">Surely to defy Israel is he coming; and whoever shall slay him, the king will enrich him with great wealth, and give him his daughter, and make his father’s house</hi> (i.e., his family) <hi type="italic">free in Israel</hi>,” viz., from taxes and public burdens. There is nothing said afterwards about the fulfilment of these promises. But it by no means follows from this, that the statement is to be regarded as nothing more than an exaggeration, that had grown up among the people, of what Saul had really said. There is al| the less probability in this, from the fact that, according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.27">1Sa 17:27</reference>, the people assured him again of the same thing. In all probability Saul had actually made some such promises as these, but did not feel himself bound to fulfil them afterwards, because he had not made them expressly to David himself.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.26-1Sam.17.27">1Sa 17:26-27</reference> <div eID="gen3953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3954" type="x-p"/> When David heard these words, he made more minute inquiries from the bystanders about the whole matter, and dropped some words which gave rise to the supposition that he wanted to go and fight with this Philistine himself. This is implied in the words, “<hi type="italic">For who is the Philistine, this uncircumcised one</hi> (i.e., standing as he does outside the covenant with Jehovah), <hi type="italic">that he insults the ranks of the living God!</hi>” whom he has defied in His army. “He must know,” says the <hi type="italic">Berleburger Bible</hi>, “that he has not to do with men, but with God. With a living God he will have to do, and not with an idol.”

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.28">1Sa 17:28</reference> <div eID="gen3954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3955" type="x-p"/> David’s eldest brother was greatly enraged at his talking thus with the men, and reproved David: “<hi type="italic">Why hast thou come down</hi> (from Bethlehem, which stood upon high ground, to the scene of the war), <hi type="italic">and with whom hast thou left those few sheep in the desert?</hi>” “<hi type="italic">Those few sheep</hi>,” the loss of only one of which would be a very great loss to our family. “<hi type="italic">I know thy presumption, and the wickedness of thy heart; for thou hast come down to look at the war</hi>;” i.e., thou art not contented with thy lowly calling, but aspirest to lofty things; it gives thee pleasure to look upon bloodshed. Eliab sought for the splinter in his brother’s eye, and was not aware of the beam in his own. The very things with which he charged his brother - presumption and wickedness of heart - were most apparent in his scornful reproof.
